canonical_question: How do the 'stack spot welds' method used by Dobbelstein et al. specifically limit the achievable geometries compared to continuous scan strategies?

question_variants.question: How do the 'stack spot welds' method used by Dobbelstein et al. specifically limit the achievable geometries compared to continuous scan strategies?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The document states that the 'stack spot welds' method is limited to forming cylindrical samples because the method involves stacking spot welds rather than creating continuous weld seams, whereas continuous scan strategies are not explicitly detailed as an alternative geometry in the provided text.

answers.answer: The provided text explicitly notes that the method used by Dobbelstein et al. (stack spot welds) is distinct from continuous weld seams and specifically limits the geometry to cylindrical samples.
answers.mechanism: stacking spot welds instead of continuous weld seams limits geometry
answers.boundary_limitation: Only cylindrical samples can be formed
evidence_spans: A PBF-LB/M machine of the type AconityMINI (Aconity GmbH, Herzogenrath, Germany) was used for manufacturing cubic samples with an edge length of 6 mm on molybdenum substrate plates obtained from Plansee SE (Reutte, Austria).
The machine is equipped with a redPower QUBE single mode fiber laser from SPI Lasers Ltd. (Southamton, UK) featuring an operating wavelength of 1080 nm and a maximum power of 1 kW.
The scanner optics used is an AxialScan-30 from Raylase GmbH (Wessling, Germany).

source_evidence_spans: Dobbelstein et al. are not welding continuous weld seams but stack spot welds onto each other to form cylindrical samples, which limits the geometries that can be manufactured
